subject: English
description: Positive, comparative, superlative; irregular forms; common transformation traps

options.option_text: gooder
better
more good
best

questions.explanation: IRREGULAR comparison: good — better — best. Not 'gooder' (incorrect) or 'more good'. Other irregulars: bad — worse — worst; little — less — least; many/much — more — most; far — farther/further — farthest/furthest. Distractor 4 = superlative.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct transformation: 'No other student in the class is as bright as Rohan' is equivalent to:

options.option_text: Rohan is bright among all students
Rohan is the brightest student in the class
Rohan is brighter than some students in class
Rohan is one of the brightest students in class

questions.explanation: 'No other X is as Y as Z' = 'Z is the Y-est X'. Positive degree negative comparison → SUPERLATIVE. 'Rohan is the brightest student'. Distractor 1 = positive (loses superlative force). Distractor 3 = comparative but weaker. Distractor 4 = 'one of the brightest' implies plural, weaker than 'no other equal'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correctly comparative form: 'Iron is _____ than aluminium.'

options.option_text: more heavier than aluminium per kilogram
heavier than aluminium of equal volume
much more heavier than aluminium per piece
heaviest among aluminium and the lighter metals

questions.explanation: Comparative of 'heavy' = HEAVIER (one-syllable + -y becomes -ier). Distractor 1 = double-comparative ('more heavier'), grammatically incorrect. Distractor 3 = same fault, even more compounded. Distractor 4 = superlative, doesn't fit 'than'.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: He is one of the most intelligent boy in his class
He is one of the most intelligent boys in his class
He is the most intelligentest boy in his class
He is more intelligent than any boys in his class

questions.explanation: 'One of the [superlative] X' — X is PLURAL because we are picking from a group. 'One of the most intelligent BOYS'. Distractor 1 wrongly singularises 'boy'. Distractor 3 = double-superlative ('mostest'), wrong. Distractor 4 = 'any boys' incorrect; should be 'any other boy in his class'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to comparative: 'Mumbai is the most populous city in Maharashtra.'

options.option_text: Mumbai is more populous than every Maharashtra city
Mumbai is more populous than any other city in Maharashtra
Mumbai is more populous than no other city in Maharashtra
Mumbai is one of the most populous cities in Maharashtra

questions.explanation: Superlative → comparative: 'X is the most Y of Z' = 'X is more Y than ANY OTHER Z'. Note 'OTHER' is essential — without it, the sentence becomes 'X is more Y than ANY Z' which would include X itself (logically impossible). Distractor 1 wrongly says 'every', includes Mumbai itself. Distractor 3 has a double-negative. Distractor 4 weakens the original superlative claim.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct comparative form: 'This book is _____ than that one.'

options.option_text: more interesting then that one
more interesting than that one
interestinger than that one
most interesting than that one

questions.explanation: Multi-syllable adjectives form comparative with 'MORE' + adjective: 'more interesting'. Connector is 'THAN' (comparison), not 'then' (temporal sequence). Distractor 1 misuses 'then'. Distractor 3 wrong inflection — multi-syllable adjectives don't take -er. Distractor 4 = superlative form (most), doesn't fit 'than'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The superlative of 'far' (when referring to distance) is:

options.option_text: farer or most far in usage
farthest, used for physical distance
more far in nearly all situations
fartest in most British English usage

questions.explanation: FAR — irregular: far / farther / farthest (physical distance) OR far / further / furthest (figurative — 'further details', 'further notice'). Distractor 1 'farer' is wrong. Distractor 3 'more far' is wrong. Distractor 4 'fartest' is incorrect spelling.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses degrees of comparison correctly?

options.option_text: The weather today is more hotter than yesterday morning.
She speaks more fluently than her sister does here.
He is more taller than the other players in the team.
This road is more wider than the one we took earlier.

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'fluently' is an adverb that forms its comparative with 'more' — no '-er' form exists, so no double comparative arises. A ('more hotter'), C ('more taller'), and D ('more wider') all commit the double comparative error: adding 'more' before an adjective that already takes the '-er' suffix (hotter, taller, wider). Only one comparative marker is permitted.

questions.stem: Convert to POSITIVE degree: 'Riya is the most diligent student in her department.'

options.option_text: No other student in her department is as diligent as Riya.
Riya is more diligent than any other student in her department.
Riya is as diligent as every other student in her department.
No other student in her department is more diligent than Riya.

questions.explanation: A is correct: the positive degree uses the 'no other … as … as' pattern, preserving superiority without any comparative or superlative form. B and D are comparative-degree equivalents ('more diligent than / more diligent than'), not positive. C inverts the meaning — 'as diligent as every other student' implies mere equality, not excellence.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an error in the use of degrees of comparison?

options.option_text: This is the most perfect arrangement we have ever seen here.
The updated software version runs far better than the older one.
Her solution was a little more elegant than his in the contest.
The committee approved a slightly improved version of the bill.

questions.explanation: A is erroneous: 'perfect' is an absolute adjective — a thing is either perfect or it is not — so it cannot be graded. 'Most perfect' is incorrect; say 'perfect' or 'nearly perfect'. B uses 'far better' correctly (far intensifies a comparative), C uses 'a little more elegant' correctly, and D uses 'slightly improved' which is not a comparison construction and is grammatically fine.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a Latin-origin comparative adjective?

options.option_text: His performance is superior than all his teammates in the squad.
The quality of this alloy is inferior to the imported alternative.
The team leader is more senior than the new recruits in the batch.
The second clause in the contract is prior than the third clause.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Latin-derived comparatives — inferior, superior, senior, junior, prior, anterior, posterior — always govern 'to', never 'than'. A uses 'superior than' (wrong preposition). C doubles the comparative by prefixing 'more' before 'senior', which is itself already a comparative form, and incorrectly uses 'than'. D uses 'prior than' instead of the correct 'prior to'.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids the illogical self-comparison error in the comparative degree?

options.option_text: This film earned more awards than any film released this decade.
This film earned more awards than any other film released this decade.
This film earned more awards than every film released in this decade.
This film won more accolades than all films put together this decade.

questions.explanation: B is correct: when comparing one member of a group to the rest of the group, 'other' must be inserted to logically exclude it from the group being compared against. Without 'other', A and C illogically include the film among its own comparators (the film earned more than itself). D's phrasing 'all films put together' shifts the comparison to a collective total, altering meaning and introducing a different logical problem.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence in which 'elder' is used INCORRECTLY.

options.option_text: Raghu is the eldest of three brothers, yet his older cousin got more.
She is elder than her husband by two years, surprising to everyone.
The elder of the two siblings secured a government post in the exam.
His elder brother, a retired colonel, still commands great respect.

questions.explanation: B is incorrect: 'elder' is never followed by 'than' in standard grammar. For direct age comparisons, 'older than' must be used. 'Elder' is reserved for family-seniority contexts (elder brother, elder sister) or as a standalone adjective/noun. A correctly uses 'older' for a direct age comparison with 'cousin'. C uses 'elder of the two' correctly (comparative selection between two people). D uses 'elder brother' correctly as a family descriptor.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a degree modifier with a comparative adjective?

options.option_text: The mountainous route is very longer than the coastal highway option.
Her revised proposal was much more persuasive than the initial draft.
The train is too faster than the bus on this particular route.
His improved score is quite better than what was initially expected.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'much' legitimately intensifies a comparative adjective ('much more persuasive'). A fails because 'very' cannot modify comparative forms; 'much longer' or 'far longer' is required. C incorrectly applies the comparative suffix '-er' after 'too' — the correct form is 'too fast', not 'too faster'. D fails because 'quite' modifies absolute or positive adjectives (quite good), not comparatives; 'somewhat better' or 'slightly better' would be grammatically correct.
